title: Correcting climate ‘misperceptions’ may not boost climate action - Carbon Brief
gist: A Nature Climate Change study of over 5,000 people in Germany and the US finds a huge attitude-behaviour gap - 37% said they would donate 1% of income to WWF, only 4% did - and that people overestimate peers' climate actions while underestimating their support. Crucially, correcting these misperceptions raised stated willingness but produced no change in actual donations, undercutting the cost-effectiveness case for norm-correction climate campaigns.

themes.theme: The attitude-behaviour gap dwarfs the perception gap

insights.claim: In survey one, 37% of participants said they were willing to donate 1% of household income to WWF but only 4% actually did when given the chance - a roughly ninefold gap between stated willingness and action.
insights.speaker: Jess Milligan
insights.so_what: Stated-preference climate surveys overstate real behaviour by close to an order of magnitude; discount consumer willingness-to-pay data in green product and ESG demand forecasts accordingly.
insights.locator: For example, survey one finds that 37%

insights.claim: The study argues the public overestimates other people's real-world climate actions while underestimating their stated support, inverting the standard one-directional 'perception gap' story.
insights.speaker: Jess Milligan
insights.so_what: The received wisdom that people simply underestimate climate support is only half right - communications strategies built on that premise are mis-specified.
insights.locator: The general public often underestimate support

insights.claim: Participants predicted 23% of peers had donated when the true figure was 4%, while estimating willingness at around 34% against an actual 37% - so overestimation of behaviour was far larger than underestimation of attitudes.
insights.speaker: Jess Milligan
insights.so_what: The measurable error is concentrated in beliefs about actions, not attitudes - a signal that social-proof campaigns citing behaviour could backfire.
insights.locator: Participants generally overestimated the climate actions

insights.claim: Prior perception-gap research relied almost entirely on self-reported willingness rather than measured behaviour such as donations, protest attendance or actual behaviour change - a methodological gap this study was designed to fill.
insights.speaker: Jess Milligan
insights.so_what: A large literature underpinning climate communications spending was built on unverified self-report; treat its policy conclusions as unproven.
insights.locator: Most studies that explore the perception gap

themes.theme: Why the misperception exists: cognition, not ideology

insights.claim: One author says the perception gap is not due to ignorance or bias but because people are simply not good at making accurate estimations about large groups.
insights.speaker: Jess Milligan
insights.so_what: Reframes the problem from a persuasion challenge to a cognitive limit - implying information campaigns aimed at correcting beliefs have a low ceiling.
insights.quote: people are just not good at making good estimations
insights.locator: One of the authors tells Carbon Brief

insights.claim: Estimates show a consistent regression to the mean, where small proportions are overestimated and large ones underestimated, pulling all predictions towards the middle regardless of the topic.
insights.speaker: Jess Milligan
insights.so_what: A general estimation bias, not a climate-specific one - the same distortion should be expected in any survey asking people to predict peer behaviour, including consumer and voter research.
insights.quote: small proportions were overestimated and large ones were underestimated

insights.claim: Individual and environmental factors also shape perceptions independently of general misestimation: people already involved in climate action, discussing climate more and consuming more climate media predicted higher climate support across the board.
insights.speaker: Jess Milligan
insights.so_what: Media diet and social exposure drive perceived norms - a channel that climate-focused media and community organising can influence, unlike raw statistics.
insights.locator: For example, people who were already involved

insights.claim: Lead author Kevin Tiede says the findings demonstrate pluralistic ignorance, where a person believes their own views differ from the majority, and that the vast majority of people worldwide support climate action but considerably underestimate the extent of that support.
insights.speaker: Jess Milligan
insights.so_what: Latent political support for climate policy is larger than the public believes - a persistent under-priced constituency for policy shifts.
insights.locator: Tiede explains that the study findings

insights.claim: Participants told that 68% of people were willing to donate 1% of household income to WWF reported more willingness to donate, but participants told that only 4% actually donated showed no increase over control.
insights.speaker: Jess Milligan
insights.so_what: Social-norm messaging only moves stated intent, and only when the norm cited is favourable - a narrow, fragile lever for behaviour-change programmes.

insights.claim: Critically, there was no obvious impact on actual donations for any of the three information groups, meaning correcting misperceptions changed talk but not money.
insights.speaker: Jess Milligan
insights.so_what: Undermines the cost-effectiveness case for norm-correction climate campaigns; funders should demand behavioural rather than attitudinal endpoints.
insights.locator: However, there was no obvious impact

insights.claim: Tiede concludes that just telling people how many people support climate action is likely not enough to really change something.
insights.speaker: Jess Milligan
insights.so_what: A direct challenge to a widely funded communications strategy - expect reallocation toward structural interventions if this replicates.
insights.quote: just telling people how many people support climate action is likely not enough to really change something
insights.locator: Lead study author Dr Kevin Tiede

insights.claim: Madalina Vascleanu of Stanford says the study is a great addition because correcting the perception gap did not affect climate-friendly behaviour as scholars had previously assumed, and it has sparked new hypotheses her lab is now pursuing.
insights.speaker: Jess Milligan
insights.so_what: Independent confirmation that a core assumption in climate behavioural science has been falsified - a research agenda now in flux.
insights.locator: Prof Madalina Vascleanu, an assistant professor

insights.claim: Vascleanu argues observable identity-signalling behaviours such as protesting or vegetarianism may influence peers more than private behaviours like donations, and that people may need to directly experience the norm rather than be told about it.
insights.speaker: Jess Milligan
insights.so_what: Visible, public consumption choices carry more social contagion than private giving - relevant to how consumer-facing green brands generate adoption.

themes.theme: Design implications: subsidise behaviour, target the supportive majority

insights.claim: The researchers argue targeted communication should focus on converting the already-supportive majority into action rather than trying to convert climate sceptics.
insights.speaker: Jess Milligan
insights.so_what: Persuasion budgets aimed at sceptics are misallocated; the marginal return is in activating existing supporters, which favours convenience-led product and policy design.
insights.locator: The researchers argue that it is more effective

insights.claim: The study recommends closing the attitude-behaviour gap by facilitating climate-friendly behaviour through convenience and subsidies rather than information alone.
insights.speaker: Jess Milligan
insights.so_what: Points to subsidy and friction-removal as the effective policy levers - supportive of demand-side incentives like heat-pump and EV subsidies over awareness campaigns.
insights.locator: The study suggests strategies for decision-makers

insights.claim: The authors also recommend that environmental policy prioritise fairness to gain visible and widespread public support, and that the public would benefit from understanding the effectiveness and co-benefits of climate action.
insights.speaker: Jess Milligan
insights.so_what: Distributional design, not messaging volume, determines political durability of climate policy - a lesson for carbon pricing and fuel-levy design.
insights.locator: They also recommend ensuring environmental policy

insights.claim: The study rests on more than 5,000 participants across Germany and the US over 2024-25, chosen as two of the top 10 CO2 emitters, but the authors acknowledge these do not reflect diverse cultural contexts.
insights.speaker: Jess Milligan
insights.so_what: Findings are drawn from two wealthy high-emitting democracies; do not extrapolate the null result on norm-correction to emerging markets.

insights.claim: Mauro Bertolotti of Universita Cattolica del Sacro Cuore is sceptical of the simplified and abstract measures, warning that experimental environments carry assumptions and expectations different from real life and may not replicate real donation decisions.
insights.speaker: Jess Milligan
insights.so_what: The headline null result may be an artefact of lab framing - watch for field replications before rewriting communications strategy.

insights.claim: Tiede himself concedes direct comparability between saying you would donate and actually donating is limited, and that more time to answer and autonomy over where to donate might produce more action.
insights.speaker: Jess Milligan
insights.so_what: The author flags that friction and choice architecture in the experiment may understate real-world giving - a caveat on the ninefold intent-action gap.
